hook.headline: Catching the exception may not save the transaction
hook.hook: With Spring REQUIRED propagation, an inner failure can mark the shared transaction rollback-only before the outer method catches it.
hook.visualCaption: The caller can continue executing while the shared physical transaction is already unable to commit.
hook.microExample: inner failure → caught outside → commit attempt → rollback

mentalModel.title: Logical scopes, one physical transaction
mentalModel.coreIdea: Each REQUIRED transactional method has a logical transaction scope, but participating scopes commonly map to the same physical transaction. If an inner scope marks that transaction rollback-only, catching its exception in the caller does not restore commit eligibility.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Control flow may recover while transaction state has already changed irreversibly for that transaction.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: inner failure → rollback-only → catch → failed commit

code.title: A catch does not clear rollback-only
code.intro: Assume reserve is a proxied REQUIRED method and its RuntimeException uses Spring's default rollback rule.
code.highlightReason: The caller catches the exception after the inner transactional interceptor can already have marked the shared transaction rollback-only.
code.takeaway: Exception handling and transaction outcome are related but separate; inspect propagation and rollback rules when reasoning about recovery.
code.professionalNote: Catching RuntimeException broadly is illustrative here, not a recommended error-handling policy for production code.

production.title: The method continues, then commit fails
production.scenario: An order service catches a failure from another REQUIRED service, logs it, performs more work and appears to recover, but the request still fails when the outer transaction completes.
problems: The inner transactional scope marked the shared physical transaction rollback-only.
Later writes in that same transaction cannot turn a rollback-only transaction back into a committable one.
production.professionalApproach: Trace calls through transactional proxy boundaries, inspect propagation and rollback rules, then decide whether the failure should abort the unit of work or needs an independent transaction or redesigned boundary.
production.debugClue: Business code reaches its final log statement, yet transaction completion throws UnexpectedRollbackException and none of the shared writes commit.

interview.question: Why can a Spring transaction still roll back after the outer service catches an exception from an inner REQUIRED method?
interview.answer: With REQUIRED propagation, the inner and outer logical transaction scopes can participate in the same physical transaction. If the inner transactional interceptor marks it rollback-only under the configured rollback rules, catching the exception later changes control flow but not that transaction state. The outer commit then rolls back and can surface UnexpectedRollbackException.
